prompt:
Genesis 1 describes six days of creation:
Day 1 – light
Day 2 – the sky, separating the waters above from the waters below
Day 3 – dry land and plants
Day 4 – sun, moon and stars
Day 5 – birds of the sky and creatures of the sea
Day 6 – land animals and people

Days 4–6 fill the spaces formed on Days 1–3. Which day fills the space formed on Day 2?
explanation: Day 2 separates the sky from the waters; Day 5 fills the sky with birds and the waters with sea creatures (1→4, 2→5, 3→6).
approach: Write the six days in two columns, Days 1–3 on the left and Days 4–6 on the right. Then read across each row and ask “what lives in what was made here?”

prompt:
In Hebrew poetry the second line often relates to the first in one of three ways:
• it repeats the idea in other words (synonymous)
• it states the opposite (antithetic)
• it adds to or completes the idea (synthetic)

“A wise son makes a glad father,
but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.” (Proverbs 10:1)

Which pattern is this?
explanation: The second line states the opposite of the first: wise/foolish, glad/sorrow.
approach: Put the two lines one above the other and pair the words in the same position. Opposite pairs: antithetic. Same meaning: synonymous. The thought moves on: synthetic. The word “but” is often a clue to contrast.

prompt:
Which name continues the pattern?

Eden, Nineveh, Hebron, ___
explanation: Each name begins with the last letter of the name before it: Eden ends in N → Nineveh; Nineveh ends in H → Hebron; Hebron ends in N → Nazareth.
approach: When the meaning of the words gives no rule (these are just places), look at their form: first and last letters, length, syllables. Check the joins between neighbours, not just each word on its own.

prompt:
In a secret code, ADAM is written as BEBN.
Using the same code, how is EVE written? Type your answer.
explanation: Each letter is replaced by the next letter of the alphabet: E→F, V→W, E→F.
approach: Compare the code letter by letter with the original and find the step for each pair. If every step is the same, apply it. Check: ADAM repeats its 1st and 3rd letter, and so does BEBN.

prompt:
Group 1 follows a rule: Ruth, Mark, Jude, Joel
Group 2 does not: Genesis, Matthew, Romans, Isaiah

Which of these book names follows the same rule as Group 1?
explanation: Every name in Group 1 has exactly four letters. Amos is the only four-letter name among the options.
approach: Look for what ALL of Group 1 share and NONE of Group 2 share. Testament, author and topic mix across both groups, so the rule must be about the words themselves. Count the letters.

prompt:
What comes next? Type the number.

3, 5, 9, 17, 33, ___
explanation: The gaps double each time: +2, +4, +8, +16, so the next gap is +32: 33 + 32 = 65.
approach: Write the gaps under the series: 2, 4, 8, 16. They double, so continue the gaps first, then add. A second route to check: each number is double the one before, minus 1 (33 × 2 − 1 = 65).

prompt:
What comes next?

2, 3, 5, 8, 12, ___
explanation: The gaps grow by one each time: +1, +2, +3, +4, then +5. 12 + 5 = 17.
approach: Write the gaps under the series: 1, 2, 3, 4. The gaps form a simple series of their own, so continue it one more step and add it on.

prompt:
What comes next?

A, C, F, J, O, ___
explanation: The steps between letters grow by one: +2, +3, +4, +5, then +6. Six letters after O is U.
approach: Turn letters into their places in the alphabet (1, 3, 6, 10, 15), solve it as a number series, then turn the answer back into a letter. Counting on from O (P, Q, R, S, T, U) is a good check.

prompt:
What comes next?

2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ___
explanation: The gaps are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next gap is 12: 30 + 12 = 42. (Each number is n × (n + 1): 1×2, 2×3, 3×4 …)
approach: Write the gaps: 4, 6, 8, 10. They go up by 2 each time, so the next gap is 12. Finding a second route to the same answer (n × (n + 1)) is a good check when a question looks hard.

prompt:
What comes next? Type the letter.

Z, X, U, Q, L, ___
explanation: Going backwards through the alphabet, the steps grow by one: −2, −3, −4, −5, then −6. Six letters before L is F.
approach: Turn the letters into numbers (A = 1 … Z = 26): 26, 24, 21, 17, 12. The gaps grow by one each time, going down. Then count six back from L: K, J, I, H, G, F.

prompt: Which word does not belong with the others?
explanation: All the others have to do with sheep. A winepress is used for making wine.
approach: Ask “what world do these words come from?” “Shepherd is the only person” leaves two other non-animals (wool, winepress), so it does not make a clean group of four.

prompt: Which number does not belong with the others?
explanation: 9, 16, 25 and 36 are square numbers (3×3, 4×4, 5×5, 6×6). 30 is not.
approach: Test common number properties in turn: even or odd, multiples of the same number, squares. Even/odd fails here (16, 30 and 36 are all even), so move on to the next test.

prompt: Which word does not belong with the others?
explanation: The others are verbs with -ing added (run, sing, walk, read). “Morning” is a noun; there is no verb “to morn”.
approach: When all the words share an ending, take it off and see what is left. Run, sing, walk and read are words; “morn” is not. Do not let a shared spelling hide a difference in grammar.

prompt: Which expression is NOT a way of saying that someone died?
explanation: The other four are polite ways of saying someone died. “Went up to Jerusalem” describes a journey.
approach: The question names the group (ways of saying someone died), so test each option against it: “could this sentence end a person’s life story?” Translators meet these polite expressions (euphemisms) often.

prompt: Which word is a different part of speech from the others?
explanation: The others are adverbs (they describe how something is done). “Holy” also ends in -ly, but it is an adjective.
approach: Put each word in a test sentence. “He walked ___” works for an adverb; “a ___ man” works for an adjective. “He walked holy” does not work. The shared “-ly” ending is the trap.

prompt:
Source text (John 1:1):
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Which back-translation clearly changes the meaning of the source?
options: In the beginning the Word already existed. The Word was with God, and the Word was God.
At the very beginning the Word was there; he was together with God, and he was God.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was a god.
Before anything else existed, there was the Word. The Word was with God and was God.
answer: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was a god.
explanation: “The Word was God” and “the Word was a god” say different things. The other three reword the verse but keep its meaning.
approach: Split the verse into its three claims: the Word existed in the beginning; was with God; was God. Check each option against all three. The option closest in wording is the one that changes the meaning: one small word can matter more than a rephrased sentence.

prompt:
Source text (Mark 1:35):
“And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed.”

Which back-translation adds something the source does not say?
options: Very early, while it was still dark, he got up, left, and went to a lonely place, where he prayed.
Very early in the morning, before daylight, he got up and went out to a deserted place to pray.
Very early, while it was still dark, he got up and went to a lonely place, where he prayed for his disciples.
Before dawn he rose, went out to an empty, lonely place, and prayed there.
answer: Very early, while it was still dark, he got up and went to a lonely place, where he prayed for his disciples.
explanation: The source says he prayed, not what he prayed for. “For his disciples” is added information.
approach: List what the source says: very early, still dark, got up, left, went to a lonely place, prayed. Tick these off in each option and underline anything left over. “Lonely”, “deserted” and “empty” all render “desolate”.

prompt:
Source text (Ruth 1:16):
“Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”

Which back-translation leaves something out?
options: I will go wherever you go and stay wherever you stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Wherever you go, I will go; wherever you live, I will live. Your people will be my people.
I will go where you go and live where you live; your people will be my people and your God my God.
Where you go, I will go; where you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people; your God will be my God.
answer: Wherever you go, I will go; wherever you live, I will live. Your people will be my people.
explanation: It drops “and your God my God”, the last and most important part of Ruth’s promise.
approach: Count the source’s parts: four promises (go, lodge, your people, your God). Count them in each option; the one with three is the answer. Check the end of a sentence carefully: omissions often happen there.

prompt:
Source text (James 1:23): “…a hearer of the word and not a doer…”

In the target language, nouns like “hearer” and “doer” sound unnatural; verbs are preferred. Which rendering keeps the meaning and uses verbs?
options: someone who listens to the word but does not do what it says
someone who both hears the word and does it
someone who does the word but does not hear it
a hearer of the word, not a doer
answer: someone who listens to the word but does not do what it says
explanation: It keeps the meaning (hears but does not do) and turns the nouns into verbs. The others change the meaning or keep the nouns.
approach: The question sets two standards: same meaning AND verbs. Test every option against the first and cross out those that fail, then test the rest against the second. Only one passes both.

prompt: A team wants to know whether readers understand their draft of a verse. Which evidence best shows that they do?
options: The translator says the verse is clear.
Three people from the community, asked “What does this verse say?”, each explained it the way the source text means it.
The draft uses about the same number of words as the source.
The verse sounds beautiful when it is read aloud.
answer: Three people from the community, asked “What does this verse say?”, each explained it the way the source text means it.
explanation: Only this option tests what readers actually understand. The others are opinions or say nothing about meaning.
approach: Ask of each option: “does this measure the thing we want to know?” The goal is reader understanding, so the best evidence comes from readers, asked an open question, checked against the source.

prompt:
Four translators – Asha, Ben, Chitra and Dev – each check one book: Ruth, Jonah, Mark or James. Ruth and Jonah are in the Old Testament; Mark and James are in the New Testament.

• Chitra checks James.
• Ben checks an Old Testament book, but not Jonah.
• Asha does not check a New Testament book.

Who checks Mark?
explanation: Chitra has James. Ben has an Old Testament book that is not Jonah, so Ruth. Asha has an Old Testament book, and only Jonah is left. That leaves Mark for Dev.
approach: Draw a small grid: names down the side, books across the top. Fill in the definite clue first (Chitra = James), then each clue that leaves only one choice. The question never mentions Dev: the answer is the person left over.

prompt:
All the members of the review team read Greek.
Some members of the review team read Hebrew.

Which statement must be true?
options: Everyone who reads Greek is on the review team.
Some people who read Greek also read Hebrew.
No one on the review team reads only Greek.
Everyone who reads Hebrew is on the review team.
answer: Some people who read Greek also read Hebrew.
explanation: The team members who read Hebrew also read Greek, because every team member does. None of the other statements follows from the two facts.
approach: Draw it: a big circle of Greek readers, the team as a circle inside it, Hebrew readers overlapping part of the team. Test each option against the picture. “All team members read Greek” does not mean “all Greek readers are on the team”.

prompt:
Read the facts, then decide for each statement:
True – it must be true
False – it cannot be true
Can't tell – it may or may not be true
passage:
Rule: Every draft that passes the community check is sent to the consultant.
The Philippians draft was sent to the consultant.
The Colossians draft was not sent to the consultant.

statements.text: The Philippians draft passed the community check.
statements.explanation: The rule does not say that only drafts that pass are sent, so the Philippians draft may have been sent for another reason.

statements.text: The Colossians draft passed the community check.
statements.explanation: If it had passed, the rule says it would have been sent. It was not sent, so it did not pass.

explanation: A rule “if passed, then sent” lets you reason from “not sent” back to “not passed”, but not from “sent” back to “passed”.
approach: Write the rule as “if passed, then sent”. “Sent” does not prove “passed” (water on the road does not prove it rained; someone may have washed a car), but “not sent” does prove “not passed”.

prompt:
A consultant checks chapters 1–5 of a book, one chapter each day from Monday to Friday.

• Chapter 3 is checked on Wednesday.
• Chapter 1 is checked the day after chapter 5.
• Chapter 2 is checked before chapter 4.
• Chapter 4 is checked after chapter 3.

Which chapter is checked on Monday?
explanation: Chapter 4 comes after Wednesday, so on Thursday or Friday. Chapters 5 and 1 need two days in a row, which leaves only Monday–Tuesday. So: Mon 5, Tue 1, Wed 3, Thu 2, Fri 4.
approach: Write Mon to Fri in a row and place the fixed clue (Wednesday = 3) first. Then place the clue that needs most room (two days in a row) and see where it still fits. Check the finished week against every clue.

prompt:
Luke 2:7: “And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.”

Which statement is NOT said in this verse?
options: She laid the baby in a manger.
There was no place for them in the inn.
The baby was wrapped in swaddling cloths.
explanation: The verse mentions an inn with no room, but no innkeeper. That detail comes from retellings, not the text.
approach: Underline the matching words for each option: “laid him in a manger”, “no place for them in the inn”, “wrapped him in swaddling cloths”. The option with nothing to underline is the answer.

prompt:
Read the verse, then decide for each statement:
True – the verse says it
False – the verse says the opposite
Can't tell – the verse does not say
passage: Matthew 2:11: “And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh.”

statements.explanation: “Going into the house” is in the verse.
Three kinds of gifts are named, but the verse does not say how many people came.

statements.text: They found the child without his mother.
statements.explanation: The verse says they saw the child “with Mary his mother”.

explanation: Separate what the verse says, what it contradicts, and what it simply does not tell us.
approach: For each statement find the matching words in the verse. Words that agree: True. Words that say the opposite: False. No words at all: Can't tell – even when tradition says otherwise.

prompt:
Mark 1:30–31: “Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them.”

Which conclusion is best supported by the text?
options: Simon’s mother-in-law asked to be healed.
The fever had lasted many days.
explanation: Having a mother-in-law means Simon had (or had had) a wife. The text says others told him about her, and says nothing about how long the fever lasted or about his wife being ill.
approach: This one asks the reverse: what can fairly be concluded. A good inference follows from the words themselves (mother-in-law → a wife); a poor one adds a new event or detail. “Best” means the strongest option, even if not 100% certain.

prompt: Genesis 1:1. Tap the word in the draft that does not match the source.
source: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
text: In the beginning, God created the heaven and the earth.
explanation: The source says “heavens” (plural); the draft has “heaven”. One missing letter changes the number.
approach: Compare word by word, including the endings: plurals, tenses and single letters are easy to miss when the sentence is familiar.

prompt:
How many differences are there between the source and the draft?

Source (Mark 11:22): And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.”
Draft: And Jesus answered him, “Have faith in Good.”
explanation: “them” became “him”, and “God” became “Good”. Everything else is the same.
approach: Both changes are a single letter, and the mind reads “Good” as “God” in a familiar phrase. Go word by word with a finger or the cursor, counting as you go, then check once more from the end backwards.

prompt:
How many times does the letter “e” appear in these words? Type the number.

Blessed are the meek
explanation: Blessed (2), are (1), the (1), meek (2): 6 in all.
approach: Count word by word and write a number for each word, then add. Counting all the words at once makes it easy to miss the double “e” in “meek” or the one at the end of “are”.

prompt: Exodus 20:13. Tap the word in the draft that does not match the source.
explanation: “Murder” became “murmur”: the words look alike, but the command now forbids grumbling (complaining) instead of killing.
approach: Words that share most of their letters slip past a quick read. Look at each word letter by letter, especially in short, familiar verses.

prompt:
Source (John 3:16): “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son…”
Draft back-translation: “For God so loved the world that he gave his Son…”

What is missing from the draft?
explanation: “His only Son” became “his Son”. (The draft also drops a comma, which does not change the meaning.)
approach: Short, familiar verses are the hardest to check, because you read them from memory. Check word by word even when you know the verse by heart.

prompt: Shepherd is to flock as ___ is to vineyard.
explanation: A shepherd takes care of a flock; a vine grower takes care of a vineyard.
approach: The sentence is “a ___ takes care of a ___”. Grape, wine and harvest belong to the vineyard, but none of them takes care of it; only a person can.

prompt: Silence is to noise as ___ is to light.
explanation: Silence is the complete absence of noise; darkness is the complete absence of light. A shadow is only a place where some light is blocked.
approach: The sentence is “___ is when there is no ___ at all”. “Shadow” is the trap: only some light is blocked. Lamp and day are sources or times of light, the opposite relationship.

prompt: Teach is to teacher as translate is to ___.
explanation: A teacher is a person who teaches; a translator is a person who translates.
approach: The relationship is between word forms: an action and the person who does it. All four options come from “translate”, so ask which form names a person. “Translation” is the thing produced.

prompt: Original painting is to copy as source text is to ___.
explanation: A copy is made from the original painting; a translation is made from the source text.
approach: The sentence is “a ___ is made from the ___”. Author, language and reader are all connected to a source text, but none of them is made from it.

prompt: Bread is to baker as ___ is to potter.
explanation: A baker makes bread; a potter makes pots. Clay is the material and the wheel and kiln are tools, not what the potter makes.
approach: Note the order: product first, then maker. The sentence is “___ is what a ___ makes”. Clay is the material, the wheel and kiln are tools: the traps are the words most strongly linked to “potter”.
